## Solution

**The answer is No.** The hypotheses do **not** imply $f \equiv 0$.

### Key observation

The conditions only constrain the Fourier transform of $f$ at **integer** frequencies. Define
$$\widehat{f}(\omega) \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\,e^{-i\omega x}\,dx .$$
Then for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$,
$$\widehat{f}(n) \;=\; \int f(x)\cos(nx)\,dx \;-\; i\int f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx ,$$
so the two given vanishing conditions are equivalent to
$$\widehat{f}(n)=0 \qquad\text{for all } n\in\mathbb{Z}.$$
The hypotheses thus say: $f\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ (taking $n=0$ gives $\int|f|<\infty$ via the absolute-value condition with $\cos(0\cdot x)=1$) and the (continuous) Fourier transform $\widehat{f}$ vanishes on the **discrete** set $\mathbb{Z}$.

A continuous function can vanish on a discrete set without being identically zero. The integer lattice is far too sparse to force $\widehat f\equiv 0$.

### Explicit counterexample

Let $g\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R})$ be any nonzero smooth bump supported in the open interval $\bigl(\tfrac14,\tfrac34\bigr)$, for instance
$$g(\omega)=\begin{cases}\exp\!\Bigl(-\dfrac{1}{1-16(\omega-\tfrac12)^{2}}\Bigr), & |\omega-\tfrac12|<\tfrac14,\\[4pt] 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
This interval contains no integer, so $g(n)=0$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, yet $g\not\equiv 0$.

Define
$$f(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} g(\omega)\,e^{i\omega x}\,d\omega .$$
Because $g$ is $C^{\infty}$ with compact support, $f$ is a **Schwartz function**: $f$ and all its derivatives decay faster than any polynomial. In particular:

1. **$f\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R})$**, and indeed $\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|f(x)\,|\,|{\sin(nx)}|\,dx<\infty$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|f(x)\,|\,|{\cos(nx)}|\,dx<\infty$ for every $n$ (bounded multipliers times an $L^{1}$ function). So the absolute-integrability hypotheses hold.

2. **$f$ is continuous** (it is even smooth).

3. By the Fourier inversion theorem (valid since $g\in L^{1}$ and $f\in L^{1}$), $\widehat{f}=g$. Hence
$$\widehat{f}(n)=g(n)=0 \qquad\text{for all } n\in\mathbb{Z},$$
which gives
$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\cos(nx)\,dx = 0 \qquad\forall\,n\in\mathbb{Z}.$$

4. **$f\not\equiv 0$**, because $g\not\equiv 0$ and the Fourier transform is injective on $L^{1}$ (if $f\equiv0$ then $\widehat f\equiv 0$, contradicting $g\not\equiv 0$). Concretely, $f(0)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int g(\omega)\,d\omega>0$ since $g\ge 0$ and is not identically zero.

### Conclusion

All the hypotheses are satisfied — continuity, the vanishing of both sine- and cosine-integrals for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, and finiteness of the corresponding absolute-value integrals — yet $f$ is a nonzero (in fact strictly positive at the origin) Schwartz function. The implication therefore **fails**.

The essential reason is that the hypotheses sample the Fourier transform only on the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}$, a set of measure zero; band-limiting $\widehat{f}$ to any open interval avoiding $\mathbb{Z}$ (such as $(\tfrac14,\tfrac34)$) produces a nonzero $f$ satisfying every condition. To force $f\equiv 0$ one would need $\widehat{f}$ to vanish on a set with an accumulation point *together with* an analyticity condition (e.g. compact support of $f$, which makes $\widehat f$ entire) — neither of which is present here.

### PROOF COMPLETE
